title: The Specificity Tree Explained (a complete guide to muscle specialization)
summary: NH lays out his tree of specificity metaphor. Lifting is a tree, each movement pattern is a branch, and the top lift of each branch is your priority. Tonnage falls like rain from the top lifts downward, and neighbouring branches carry over to each other. He uses it to organise exercise selection, prioritisation, recovery and supersets.
claims: Before choosing a template or frequency, build your exercise list; all programming variables (volume, intensity, frequency) apply to movement patterns

Picture lifting as a tree whose branches are movement patterns (knee flexion, hip hinge, vertical pull...); neighbouring branches like knee flexion and hip hinge are more related than distant ones like hinge and vertical pull
The top of each branch is your most important lift, chosen subjectively (e.g. deadlift for the hinge), and the hierarchy below it must be respected
Lifts near the top should be the most specific to the king lift because they must feed it most
Tonnage falls like rain from the top lift down the branch; lifts at the bottom carry over little to the top and get less frequency, volume and intensity
Lifts low on a branch often carry over more to their own top lift than a neighbouring branch's top lift does: the RDL and back extension carry over to the deadlift more than the squat does
Some lifts carry over to two neighbouring branches, e.g. the good morning helps both squat and deadlift
Distant branches do not carry over: no horizontal press helps the deadlift; overhead press carries over to bench more than flies
Isolation movements belong on the tree at the bottom of branches; a bodybuilder needs them but they get less attention than compounds
Map every lift you do onto the tree; if you understand it you control it, otherwise it controls you
Branches for prioritized body parts sit higher and catch the tonnage first, so they get better quality and quantity; if they do not grow faster your volume scheduling is wrong
Perfectly equal development of every body part is unrealistic because of genetics and preferences
As a branch grows with work capacity, it holds more variations, which helps prevent overuse injuries; but 20 exercises is too many and neurological adaptations cannot be maintained
Branch capacity is measured in tonnage, not number of lifts: squat, paused squat and front squat can produce as much tonnage as five or more upper-body pressing lifts
Do not get greedy; uneven branches are fine as long as progression continues, and growth should stay proportionate
Lower-body branches carry a higher recovery cost than upper-body ones, which affects frequency
Flies barely affect deadlift recovery, while squats do damage hinge performance
Understanding carryover shows where to fit tonnage into supersets at no recovery cost, which becomes necessary when 4-minute rests between sets are no longer feasible
If you understand what a lift does but not what it does to its neighbours, you do not really understand the lift
